text:
Priya: Hey folks — ran a couple of nsys captures on the KV-prefetch microbenchmark and seeing a weird pattern: GPU kernels and H2D copies *look* to overlap, but every ~12ms there is a 5-20ms gap where the GPU is idle and nothing is executing. timeline looks like memcpy/kernel/memcpy/kernel... then a pause where the host thread is blocked and the next kernel is delayed. Anyone seen periodic CPU scheduling gaps like this? :thinking:

Sam: can you paste the nsys command you used and a tiny text extract of the timeline (kernel durations & memcpy durations)? that helps narrow if it's an implicit sync or host-side scheduling.

Priya: command was:
```
nsys profile --trace=cuda,cudnn,osrt --sample=cpu --output=kv-prefetch-1 ./bin/kv_prefetch --bs=8 --seq=1024 --runs=200
```
Timeline summary (rough):
- memcpy H2D 0.9ms
- kernel A 1.3ms
- memcpy H2D 1.1ms
- kernel B 1.6ms
- idle gap 12ms (host sleeping)
- memcpy H2D 0.8ms
- kernel A 1.2ms
- ... repeat
I can upload the qdrep if needed.

Jorge: hmm. two quick possibilities: 1) pageable host buffers causing implicit synchronous staging copies that interact badly with the runtime, 2) host thread getting preempted (futex/clk_nanosleep) while it's preparing the next launch, causing those 12ms windows. Did you use pinned host memory / cudaHostAlloc or plain new/malloc?

Priya: currently using std::vector + cudaMemcpyAsync (we thought async was enough). We weren't pinning the buffers. :grimacing:

Sam: that explains a lot. cudaMemcpyAsync with pageable memory triggers an implicit staged copy that can be synchronous relative to host scheduling. When the host thread is descheduled (scheduler slice), the staged copy and subsequent kernel launch can be delayed. Two quick tests:
- test A: switch to pinned memory (cudaHostAlloc) and re-run nsys
- test B: while running, attach with perf and watch futex/clock_nanosleep syscalls: `strace -f -e futex,clock_nanosleep -p <pid>` or `perf record -p <pid>` to see kernel/host sleeps

Jorge: also check if you're accidentally using the default stream anywhere — implicit syncs happen across default stream and some memcopies. Make sure kernels and memcopies are all on an explicit cudaStream_t.

Priya: ran test A (pinned). gap dropped from ~12ms to ~2ms and the idle windows are mostly gone. 👍

Sam: nice. That matches the pageable->staging hypothesis. For long-term:
- use pinned buffer pool / cudaHostAlloc + reuse
- if you need malloc-like semantics, consider cudaHostRegister at allocation time
- use cudaMemcpyAsync(..., stream) and avoid default stream
- if prefetching from CPU, try(cudaMemPrefetchAsync + stream) on unified mem for devices that support it

Jorge: another angle — if you still see small periodic gaps, they might be due to CPU scheduling for the host-side feeder work (VLAs parsing, GC in runtime, Python GIL if applicable). For that, try pinning the host feeder thread to a dedicated core and boost priority temporarily:
```
sched_setaffinity(0, mask);
chrt -f 20 ./bin/kv_prefetch ...
```
If gaps disappear, you likely need a lighter host-side work path or isolate the feeder thread.

Priya: interesting — we run this inside a worker process spawned by our runtime. I did `taskset -c 10` to pin the thread and the gaps vanished. With both pinned host buffers + CPU pinning, end-to-end p99 latency dropped ~18%.

Sam: great! A couple of profiling nitpicks for future captures:
- run `nsys profile --trace=cuda,cudnn,osrt,osrt_cpu` and capture NVTX ranges: instrument critical sections with NVTX so timeline ranges are easy to filter
- use `--capture-range=nvtx` around the steady-state to reduce noise
- enable `--sample=cpu` to get host stack samples (helps spot blocking syscalls)

Priya: thanks — will add NVTX around the prefetch/fill/launch loop. Also saw a weird kernel selection issue where a slower quantized kernel got picked for some sequence lengths. Any tips to correlate chosen kernel variant in nsys?

Jorge: include kernel names + module names in the timeline, and search for the kernel that matches the slow variant (sometimes name suffixes like _q8 or _f16). Also instrument the runtime to log kernel variant decisions (model, seq_len, kernel_id) to stdout/NVTX at decision time so you can join logs with the timeline.

Sam: and for batching heuristics — if you see big variance tied to batch boundary events, add an NVTX marker at the batching decision and capture the batch size used per launch. That often shows perf cliffs when small vs medium batch kernels chosen.

Priya: plan: 1) patch to use pinned pool + explicit streams, 2) NVTX around batch decision + kernel selection logging, 3) rerun nsys with capture-range=nvtx and sample=cpu, 4) if any remaining gaps file perf regression ticket with trace attached. I'll drop qdrep in #eng-runtime once I have it.

Sam: sounds good. Optional next optim: pre-allocate a small pool of pinned pages and use cudaStreamBeginCapture to bench ordering if you suspect stream dependency overheads.

Priya: will try. thanks all :pray: — uploading trace in ~1h.
